user.title: Dayline
user.description:
Nothing here is required. Submit as-is and every calendar in this instance goes on the spine, so you get a real day immediately.

To narrow it, apply the **Dayline** label to the calendars you want under [Settings → Areas & labels](/config/labels) — labelled calendars replace this list entirely, take effect without a restart, and mean adding a calendar next month never involves Dayline at all. The list below is only the fallback for anyone who would rather answer a question than apply a label.

data.calendars: Calendars (optional — the Dayline label is the better way)

labels.title: Labels and tags

sources.title: Weather and to-do
sources.description:
The weather entity supplies the hourly forecast joined onto upcoming entries; the to-do list supplies the sticky rows with a Done button. One of each — these are genuine choices, not something a label can answer.

The calendar list below is the fallback only. If anything carries the **Dayline** label, this list is not consulted at all.

calendars.title: Calendar wording
calendars.description:
The {count} calendars currently on the spine. This is the one thing about a calendar a label cannot say for you.

The label is what the pill in the legend says; calendars sharing a label share a pill. Order matters: when two calendars carry the same event worded differently, the first listed supplies the wording — and its colour.

Colour answers *who*, since the spine already answers what and when: it tints the calendar's pill and the dot beside each of its entries. Home Assistant does not pass a calendar's own colour through from CalDAV or Google — there is no field for it on a calendar entity — so this is where it is chosen. Terracotta and sage are not on the list: they already mean “now” and “the house acting on its own”.

Set the role to “schedule” for a calendar that drives automations rather than describing people's plans — its events become House rows and each event's description becomes the sage sentence.

To add or remove a calendar, apply or remove the **{label}** label rather than editing anything here.

sentences.title: Sentences
sentences.description:
What the house will do, in plain words, matched against any text in an event's title. First match wins, so order is precedence.

This describes; it does not act. To make an event actually do something, put a `#tag` in its title instead — see “Labels and tags”.

sentence_edit.title: Sentence
sentence_edit.description: Say the consequence, not the scene name: “Entry unlocks on her arrival”, not “scene.arrival_1”.

data.sticky: Stays until someone acts on it

recent.title: What just happened
recent.description:
Short-lived lines explaining changes the house made on its own, and only when something other than a person caused the change.

Which entities can produce one is decided by the **{label}** label, not by this list. A labelled entity with no line here still gets a serviceable sentence built from its own name — this is where you write a better one.

Currently labelled:

{watched}

recent_edit.title: Explanation
recent_edit.description: One sentence per entity per state. Plain words, no entity ids. The entity still needs the **Dayline** label for this to ever fire.

leaving.title: Leaving
leaving.description:
When an event says where it is, Dayline can work out when you have to leave: the drive at the time you would be driving it, plus a buffer for parking and walking in.

There is nothing to install. This uses Home Assistant’s own Waze Travel Time component — no account and no API key — and Dayline loads it only to ask the question. No extra sensor appears.

It is the one thing here that talks to a server outside your house, which is why it is off until you turn it on. Only the next few events are priced, and only the ones whose location looks like a place: “Zoom” and “TBD” are left alone.

Start from can be an address, a latitude and longitude, or an entity — `zone.home` for the house, or a person to route from wherever they are.

tuning.title: Tuning
tuning.description:
Similarity is how much of two titles must match before they are treated as one event — 0.8 is strict. Lower it if duplicates slip through, raise it if unrelated events start merging.

“Check calendars every” is also how promptly a `#tag` can fire: a tag added to an event starting sooner than that may miss its moment.

Leave the templates empty for sensible defaults.

data.min_gap: Name clear time of at least

data_description.min_gap: A day of six events looks full whether or not there is a clear three hours in the middle of it, and the three hours is usually what is being looked for. Gaps this long or longer get a row of their own, measured from now — so a gap half spent says what is left of it rather than what it was at lunchtime. Only calendar events count: sunset is not somewhere you have to be. Set to 0 to switch it off.

alarms.title: Alarms, and what happens when today is spent
alarms.description:
The next alarm on each phone, from the Home Assistant Companion app.

The sensor ships switched off. On each phone: Settings → Companion app → Manage sensors → Next alarm. Until that is on, there is nothing here to find.

An alarm going off today sits at its own time. One past midnight is held back until nothing else is left in the day, so tomorrow's 6:30 never sits above tonight's dinner — and the same rule can carry tomorrow's first commitments.

There is no cutoff hour in any of this. The day pivots when it is actually over, which is the only version that works if you are on nights.

data.alarm_horizon: Show an alarm up to this far ahead
data.alarm_packages: Only these apps (leave empty for all)
data.tomorrow: Show tomorrow once today is done

data_description.alarm_entities: One per phone — look for “Next alarm”.
data_description.alarm_horizon: Sixteen hours carries an evening across to a morning alarm and no further. Without a cap, an alarm set for Monday would sit on a Friday-night panel announcing Monday.
data_description.alarm_packages: Anything using Android's alarm clock lands in that sensor — a bedtime reminder, a fitness app. The row names the app that set it, so add its package name here to keep it, or leave this empty and keep them all.
data_description.tomorrow: At eleven at night “nothing else today” is true and answers the wrong question. With this on, the card names what tomorrow starts with instead. Held back entirely while today still has something left in it, so a day in progress looks exactly as it does now. All-day events are left out — they carry no time, and the only thing being asked out here is when tomorrow starts.
data_description.tomorrow_horizon: Counted from now, not from midnight. Sixteen hours carries an evening across to the next working morning and no further, so a Friday-night panel does not start announcing Monday.
